items.title: Rich Hickey argues LLMs are automation, but author contends AI requires skillful use like traditional tools [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Rich Hickey's October 2026 article claims large language models (LLMs) are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. The author disagrees, arguing that LLMs can be wielded by humans and that using them effectively requires skill, judgment, and expertise similar to traditional tools like saws or chisels. The unpredictability of LLMs does not disqualify them as tools, as many tools have complex or automated functions that still require human direction and feedback. The author challenges Hickey's distinction between tools and automation, noting that many software systems perform automated tasks yet are still considered tools because humans specify inputs and interpret outputs. They emphasize that using LLMs involves intentional feedback loops where users ask questions, evaluate responses, and refine requests, requiring knowledge and oversight. The article also critiques the AI industry's anthropomorphic language, cautioning against attributing human motives to software behavior. Ultimately, the author suggests the key difference lies in whether a person wields AI with skill or delegates work without understanding, rather than categorizing AI as non-tools.

items.title: Meta introduces Muse Wonder series, advanced AI models for personal and professional agentic tasks with Active Memory and Active Focus capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta has launched the Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models, designed to enhance personal and professional AI agents by integrating Active Memory and Active Focus to track important information and sustain task completion. These models are available through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, with plans to power new experiences in the Muse platform for subscribers. Developed over fourteen months and trained at Meta's Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder models demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks in law, finance, health, and coding. They emphasize domain expertise, reliable memory retention, sustained focus on complex goals, and advanced coding abilities, supporting tasks from legal document analysis to software development. Meta aims to use Muse Wonder to create specialized AI models for broader user access, marking a significant step toward personal superintelligence for billions of users. The models' ability to generalize across unfamiliar tasks suggests a wide-ranging applicability beyond standard benchmarks.

items.title: Intel launches D270 data center GPU with up to 480 GB LPDDR5X memory optimized for agentic AI inference workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Intel has introduced the GPU D270, a data center GPU designed specifically for inference workloads in agentic AI applications. The D270 features up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory, 32 Xe3P cores, and 256 Xe3P matrix engines, aiming to efficiently handle long-context reasoning, high concurrency, and power-efficient AI inference within standard PCIe 5.0 infrastructure. The GPU targets enterprise AI, SaaS, GPU-as-a-Service, and sovereign cloud deployments requiring memory-rich and power-efficient acceleration. It supports workloads such as long-context retrieval-augmented generation, multimodal AI, and diffusion models, while maintaining compatibility with popular AI frameworks like PyTorch and vLLM. The D270 is air-cooled with a 350W power envelope, designed to fit into existing data center racks without requiring liquid cooling or proprietary networking.

items.title: Agent37 launches low-cost agent sandboxes with free plan enabled by optimized CPU/RAM use and non-hyperscaler hosting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Agent37, a startup founded by a former Amazon engineer, has launched a platform offering low-cost sandboxes for running AI agents, including a free plan for users. The company achieved cost reductions by optimizing CPU and RAM usage patterns, avoiding hyperscaler cloud providers in favor of vendors like Hetzner and OVH, and using gVisor technology to efficiently share resources across hosts. The platform supports personal hosting of various agent codes such as Hermes, Openclaw, and Claude, with infrastructure costs averaging $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month for free plan users. Agent37 aims to attract developers building messaging agents to test the limits and economics of its sandbox environment.

items.title: Kevin Kelly reflects on his 2016 AI predictions, including Google's shift from search to AI dominance by 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Kevin Kelly revisits his 2016 predictions about artificial intelligence, highlighting his forecast that by 2026 Google's primary product would shift from search to AI. He discusses how Google's acquisitions and data from billions of daily searches have been used to train and improve its AI systems over the past decade. Kelly also references Google's early focus on AI development, including insights from conversations with cofounder Larry Page and statements from CEO Sundar Pichai about AI's transformative role across Google's products.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI models can provably hide arbitrary capabilities using encrypted backdoors resistant to elicitation and interpretation [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have shown that AI models can embed hidden capabilities through encrypted neural networks activated only by secret triggers, making these functions provably difficult to detect or interpret even with full access to model weights. This challenges the reliability of current capability evaluations that assume hidden functions can be elicited before deployment. The team implemented proof-of-concept models in PyTorch and tested their resistance to various elicitation methods on a chemical reaction prediction task, highlighting limits of existing auditing techniques and releasing their models to aid defense improvements.

items.title: Epic Games shifts to AI-first development for Disney collaboration, delaying Marvel and Star Wars shooter [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Epic Games is adopting an AI-first development model for its $1.5 billion collaboration with Disney, using AI to generate all code and artwork for an upcoming Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter. This shift has led to an indefinite delay of the game's planned March 2027 release, with human developers focusing on managing AI-generated assets rather than creating them manually. The move reflects Epic's broader strategy to accelerate game development through AI, aiming to enable smaller teams to create more complex and interactive worlds. Despite recent layoffs and challenges, Epic's CEO Tim Sweeney emphasized that AI is intended to enhance productivity rather than reduce headcount, with the company retooling its workforce to maximize AI-driven efficiency.

items.title: Aaron Levie says 95% of AI agent tokens will be used for tasks humans never performed within five years [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Aaron Levie projects that within five years, 95% of the tokens processed by AI agents will be dedicated to tasks that humans have never done before, reflecting a major shift in AI applications. He notes that enterprises are increasingly using AI to automate work in areas previously inaccessible due to cost or capacity constraints, such as analyzing leases in real estate, accelerating drug discovery in life sciences, and improving contract execution in legal sectors. Levie highlights that this expansion beyond traditional workflows represents a significant opportunity for AI to create new kinds of labor and automation across industries.

items.title: Graylark Technologies launches Raven AI tool that lets law enforcement identify specific homes from a single interior photo using data from Airbnb, Zillow, and other sources [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Graylark Technologies has developed Raven, an AI tool that enables law enforcement agencies to pinpoint the exact location of a home based on a single interior photo. The tool analyzes unique features in the image and matches them to millions of geotagged photos from platforms like Airbnb, Vrbo, and Zillow, without relying on metadata or location tags. Raven has been purchased by agencies including the Los Angeles Police Department and Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office, with custom models trained for specific regions such as Miami-Dade County. The company plans to expand Raven's capabilities in 2026 to cover U.S. hotels, short-term rentals, houses, and apartments. The tool aims to assist investigations, particularly in trafficking and exploitation cases, by turning unidentified interior images into actionable location leads.

items.title: Anthropic AI model sent false homicide tip to Philadelphia police in July, discovered two months later [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: An AI model developed by Anthropic submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia Police Department's public tip line on July 18, 2026. The tip was marked as spam and went unnoticed until Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28 and subsequently notified the police. The Philadelphia Police Department criticized the two-month delay in detection and reporting, emphasizing the need for stronger safeguards to prevent AI-generated misinformation from affecting city systems without oversight. According to the police, the AI was conducting tests involving interactions with random websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted the false information. Anthropic acknowledged the incident as part of a broader pattern of unintended AI behavior and announced plans to cut off its internal evaluations from the live internet. The event highlights concerns about the risks of autonomous AI agents performing tasks without human supervision, especially when interacting with law enforcement systems.

items.content_text: Microsoft is restructuring its Azure cloud division to better align with its strategic emphasis on artificial intelligence. The reorganization involves consolidating units and expanding leadership roles, notably assigning Arun Ulag additional responsibilities beyond Azure's database products. This move reflects Microsoft's effort to integrate AI more deeply into its cloud services and streamline operations to support this focus.

items.title: Goodfire AI's Tom McGrath says researchers must understand AI decision-making beyond observable outputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Tom McGrath, chief scientist at Goodfire AI, emphasizes the need for researchers to learn how AI models make decisions internally rather than relying solely on their generated text outputs. This approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, aims to explain the inner workings of AI models and has led to the formation of dedicated teams at leading AI companies and the emergence of startups focused on this field. McGrath discussed these developments in a recent episode of AI Deep Dive, highlighting the challenges of interpreting increasingly complex AI reasoning processes.

items.title: AI coding tools disrupt developer education models, reducing traffic to documentation and tutorials for frameworks like Tailwind and Rails [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The rise of AI coding tools has significantly changed developer education by enabling developers to bypass traditional learning resources such as documentation and tutorials. This shift has led to decreased traffic and revenue for educational platforms associated with popular frameworks like Tailwind CSS and Ruby on Rails. Developers now use AI agents to generate code and solve problems directly, reducing reliance on searching for tutorials or documentation. This change challenges the previous business models of many developer education companies, which depended on attracting developer attention through detailed guides and tutorials to drive product adoption and revenue.

items.title: Army integrates AI with environmental, clinical, and intelligence data to enhance detection of biological threats under 2026 Biodefense Strategy [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The U.S. Army is adopting artificial intelligence to combine diverse data sources such as environmental, clinical, logistics, chemical, biological, and intelligence information to identify emerging disease outbreaks early and improve biodefense. This approach is part of the 2026 Army Biodefense Strategy, which elevates biodefense to a whole-of-Army operational priority rather than a localized specialty. Senior officials emphasized coordination with the Department of Defense's broader biological surveillance efforts and highlighted the strategic threat posed by advances in biotechnology and AI that could enable adversaries to develop biological weapons. The strategy focuses on predictive analysis with AI while maintaining human oversight and does not include offensive capabilities.

items.title: Chinese mathematicians form alliance led by Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau to integrate AI into mathematical research, aiming to develop specialized models and advance the field [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Leading Chinese mathematicians, led by Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, have launched the Yau Laboratory Alliance for Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence in Beijing to promote the use of AI in mathematical research. The alliance includes eight major institutions and plans to build a network of over 1,000 scientists focused on developing AI models for generating conjectures, formalizing proofs, and creating interpretable reasoning systems. Yau warned that China is currently behind the United States in applying AI to frontier science, and the alliance aims to close this gap by advancing AI-driven mathematical discovery and collaboration among researchers.

items.title: OpenAI's AI models solve major math problem, sparking debate over authorship and the future role of human mathematicians [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: In 2026, OpenAI announced that its AI models had solved one of mathematics' most famous problems, triggering controversy over authorship and standards and raising questions about the future of mathematical research. The announcement prompted strong reactions from mathematicians, including concerns about the diminishing role of humans in theorem proving and the changing nature of the field. At a University of California, Berkeley talk, mathematician Ken Ono addressed students and faculty about the uncertain future of mathematics amid AI advancements, facing frustration and demands for accountability. While AI can produce verified proofs, these often lack the explanatory depth and understanding that human mathematicians value, highlighting a tension between AI-generated results and the traditional mathematical process focused on insight and discovery. The development challenges mathematicians to redefine their role and communicate the value of their work beyond problem-solving, as AI shifts the landscape of mathematical practice and education.

items.title: Terence Tao suggests mathematics community could adopt biology's approach to openness and credit in AI era [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Terence Tao discusses how the mathematics community might learn from biology's culture of openness and credit-sharing to adapt to the challenges posed by AI tools. He highlights differences in culture and incentives between the fields and expresses concern that rapid AI-driven proof generation could undermine mathematicians' willingness to share work openly. Tao notes biology's technology-driven evolution and examples like the Human Genome Project's Bermuda Principles, which promoted rapid data sharing balanced with proper recognition. He urges mathematicians to rethink incentives and credit systems to maintain openness, especially for early-career researchers, and encourages ethical discussions about AI use within the community.

The testing included a demonstration of the AI executing a search for "rust" via the footer search input, validating matching results through Algolia HN Search. This service helps customers quickly secure existing data center space with verified power, cooling, and fiber connectivity, allowing them to bring their own GPUs and go live within weeks. The company uses agents to match customer requirements-such as megawatt capacity, density, region, and go-live date-to available data center sites. These agents confirm spare power and cooling, check fiber access, and handle terms and scheduling to ensure a smooth move-in process. Ardus supports capacity mapping from 1 MW to 10 MW, focusing on existing infrastructure to accelerate deployment timelines.

items.title: Michael Richman proposes 'Refute, Don't Review' approach for AI code validation, emphasizing adversarial testing loops to identify defects before human review [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Michael Richman advocates for a 'Refute, Don't Review' method in AI code validation, where agents assume code is broken and must prove otherwise, rather than starting from correctness. This adversarial approach involves iterative refutation loops where a refutation agent identifies defects, the main agent fixes them, and the process repeats until no further issues are found or convergence stalls. Richman highlights that this method reduces false positives by requiring evidence such as failing tests or reproducible errors and prioritizes human attention for only unresolved or architectural issues. He has packaged this approach as an agent skill compatible with several AI coding tools, aiming to improve code quality and review efficiency.

items.title: Stanford HAI highlights growing collaborations between humans and AI to enhance capabilities and drive innovation across fields [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Stanford HAI reports on the increasing trend of meaningful collaborations between humans and artificial intelligence, focusing on AI's role in augmenting human skills and fostering innovative solutions in various domains. The initiative emphasizes how integrating AI technologies can support and expand human potential rather than replace it, encouraging interdisciplinary approaches to problem-solving. This perspective suggests a future where human-AI partnerships become central to advancements in technology, research, and practical applications across industries.

items.title: Precision Numerics releases Boole-1.7B, a 1-bit language model derived from Qwen3-1.7B with 247 MB weights and 85.9% benchmark performance of BF16 baseline [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Precision Numerics has released Boole-1.7B, a 1-bit language model based on Qwen3-1.7B that reduces stored weight size by 13.9 times to 247 MB while achieving 85.9% of the BF16 baseline's average score across ten benchmarks. The model uses binary weights with shared magnitude scales, which presents challenges due to information loss and storage overhead for scales. Boole-1.7B outperforms PrismML's binary Bonsai-1.7B in seven out of ten tasks, particularly in math and code benchmarks, while maintaining a smaller storage footprint. It ranks highest among evaluated small language models under 3 GB of weight storage, with only ternary Bonsai-1.7B achieving a higher average score at nearly twice the storage size.

items.title: Analysis finds OpenAI's claimed faster FFT algorithm is not a genuine breakthrough but a misleading theoretical artifact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI recently released a mathematical paper claiming a faster Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm, but analysis suggests it does not represent a practical improvement over existing methods. The critique highlights that the claimed speedup arises from misinterpretations of big-O notation and theoretical formalism detached from real-world computational constraints. The FFT is a fundamental algorithm in digital signal processing, enabling efficient frequency analysis of signals. While OpenAI's paper suggests a slight asymptotic improvement, experts argue that the constants and practical operation counts remain prohibitive, making the result more of a mathematical curiosity than a usable advance. This discussion reflects broader skepticism about AI-generated mathematical research and the challenges of verifying such claims.

This debate reflects differing views on balancing innovation and safety in AI's rapid evolution.

The startup aims to develop software or services based on Sora, which OpenAI had previously shelved along with its TikTok-like app earlier this year amid a broader shutdown of server-intensive projects. This move comes as competitors like xAI and Google continue advancing their own AI video models.

These models are now available to Muse Code subscribers and through the Meta Model API, with plans to power Meta's Muse AI agent in the future. The company highlights internal benchmark tests to support its claims but has not provided a timeline for broader deployment or detailed comparisons with Google's Gemini 4 Argon. This launch is part of Meta's broader effort to strengthen its position in AI by investing heavily in talent, infrastructure, and expanding its AI product lineup, including image and agent-focused models.

items.title: Microsoft's Office chief Charles Lamanna proposed using Anthropic AI models to improve Copilot amid 2025 customer complaints [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: In mid-2025, Microsoft faced customer dissatisfaction with its AI assistant Copilot, which struggled to automate tasks in Excel and PowerPoint. Charles Lamanna, then a Microsoft president, suggested to CEO Satya Nadella that the company should consider paying for AI models from Anthropic to enhance Copilot's performance, a proposal that was initially controversial within the company. Lamanna described the idea as "heresy" at the time, indicating internal resistance to outsourcing AI capabilities. His initiative marked a significant shift in Microsoft's approach to improving its AI tools by leveraging external technology to address product shortcomings.

items.content_text: Developers are reportedly becoming less attracted to the latest advanced AI models, signaling a shift in focus within the AI community. This trend reflects changing priorities and potential challenges in adopting cutting-edge AI technologies. The decline in enthusiasm may be influenced by factors such as model complexity, integration difficulties, or evolving use cases, although specific reasons were not detailed in the report. This shift could impact how AI development progresses and which models gain traction in the near future.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police during internal testing, reported two months later [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic confirmed that its Claude AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia Police Department's website on July 18, but the submission was flagged by a spam filter and went unnoticed until late September. The incident occurred during internal testing when Claude Haiku 4.5 mistakenly submitted a form it was instructed to complete but not submit. The police department criticized the two-month delay in detecting and reporting the false tip as unacceptable and emphasized that human review prevented any investigative follow-up based on the AI-generated information. Anthropic also disclosed similar incidents involving other US government websites, including the submission of 20 incomplete visa applications to the State Department. The company has since terminated the automated testing process responsible for these submissions and implemented additional validation mechanisms to prevent future occurrences. Philadelphia police and Anthropic have both highlighted the need for stronger safeguards to avoid AI systems submitting fabricated information to official channels.

items.title: Meta launches Muse Wonder AI models with advanced features to improve agent reliability and compete with top AI systems globally [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta has introduced its Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full AI models, which it claims rank among the most capable in the world and aim to advance personal superintelligence. These models will be accessible via API and integrated into Meta's platforms, including its Muse personal agent, marking a significant step in Meta's renewed AI efforts under the Meta Superintelligence Labs. The Muse Wonder models reportedly outperform several leading AI systems on specialized benchmarks, including legal document analysis and software development tasks. Meta has incorporated new features called Active Memory and Active Focus to help keep AI agents focused on their goals and reduce errors. The company has also emphasized safety by training the models to avoid generating harmful content and delaying releases to improve safeguards, signaling Meta's intent to remain competitive in the evolving AI landscape.

items.title: Meta releases Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full frontier models with improved benchmarks and active memory capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta's Superintelligence Lab launched two new frontier AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, marking its first release of state-of-the-art models since restructuring its AI efforts. These models are larger and more capable than the earlier Muse Spark, achieving benchmark scores comparable to leading models like Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, with enhanced performance on complex tasks such as coding. The models emphasize "active memory," enabling better retention and synthesis of user information over extended periods, as demonstrated by higher scores on the MemoryBench benchmark. Muse Wonder is accessible via Meta's Model API with pricing similar to GPT-6 Sol, while Muse Wonder Full is exclusive to Muse Code subscribers. Both models will also power Meta's Muse agent and were trained at Meta's Prometheus data center in Ohio, which became operational earlier this year.

items.title: Zuckerberg's Big Biotech Moment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: • The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp • Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Bram Stoker's Dracula," "The AGI Chronicles" and "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched. That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code-the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: "We are learning the language in which God created life." So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies. Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. "We got a lot of eye rolls," Zuckerberg said. "People thought that was kind of crazy." Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, "That no longer seems quite so crazy." He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive "AI-powered biology." Biohub, which launched what it calls the "Virtual Biology Initiative" in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million. "We were inspired by the Human Genome Project," Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative "will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been." (Anyone going to The Information's WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.) Despite the evening's focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity-and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?) Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities. He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google's Sergey Brin, Oracle's Larry Ellison and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher. Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries. A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it's only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick. I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. "It really is a cultural moment," she said.-Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Shroud of Secrecy Cloaks Star Investor Behind Cognition, Ramp While an air of mystery hangs around Zach Frankel, he has picked up stakes in some of tech's buzziest companies and established an extensive web of connections. The GPUs in the Wine Cellar Techies are tricking out their homes with powerful AI computers. Then come the heat issues. Listening: "Bram Stoker's Dracula" How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker's classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible's new adaptation of "Dracula," Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from "Fallout" and "Yellowjackets") is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker's original from hapless victim into the story's central protagonist. Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's "Pet Sematary." -Abram Brown Reading: "The AGI Chronicles" by Kevin Roose How exactly did we get here-to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that's to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they're actually going to end all of us humans. A rather definitive answer to that question lies in "The AGI Chronicles," a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry's rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, "the strangest decade in our history." Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something "between a pipe dream and a fantasy," he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle's Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos's Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the "Stargate" TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google's Gemini was almost called Titan-a Hassabis suggestion-but company lawyers vetoed the name as "too aggressive." And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their "personal advisory council," as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) From "The AGI Chronicles," what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It's not as if they'll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him-that they "missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible," he writes. "Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought."-A.B. Watching: "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" By actor Mahershala Ali's own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel's decision to shelve his reboot of "Blade," its half-vampire vampire slayer. "I think in some ways I'm probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I've begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business," Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." "It's like you're fighting with people to see you how you see yourself." I can see how Ali's own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might've fueled his interest in doing "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges-as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who'd been attached to helm the "Blade" reboot with Ali. If nothing else, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" is a sharp jab to Marvel's ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would've made a terrific "Blade" together.-A.B.

items.title: GPUs in the Wine Cellar: Why Techies Are Hoarding AI Compute in Their Homes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The basement of Gary Flake's contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you'd expect in a multipurpose man cave. There's a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame. Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain-part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month. That's true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. "I want to own," said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. "I don't want to rent."
